title: Well-log layer segmentation
intro: Well logs continuously measure rock properties along a borehole. Dividing these curves into geological units provides the reference boundaries for reservoir interpretation, perforation intervals and stimulation stages. Errors in this first step propagate into downstream decisions.

sections.title: Current practice and challenges
sections.html:
Interpreters compare several curves and nearby wells over long intervals. The original case describes 2–4 hours of manual work per well and differences of 0.5–1 m between interpreters. Thin interbeds make boundaries particularly ambiguous.

Different interpreters may also disagree on the number of layers. Evaluation should therefore match boundaries within a depth tolerance rather than score every sample as a classification problem.

sections.title: What AI can do
sections.html:
Frame the task as change-point detection. Windowed statistics, optimal segmentation or a 1D segmentation model generate candidate boundaries; geological rules then filter implausible results.

The algorithm narrows a long log to a reviewable set of candidates. Interpreters remain responsible for geological validity. Minimum layer thickness and consistency with neighboring wells are central constraints.

sections.title: Data preparation
sections.html:
• GR, SP, RT and DEN logs, aligned at 0.125 m sampling; the source case proposes 5,000–20,000 samples per well and manual layer tables for 30–50 wells.
  • Layering and lithology from more than 20 neighboring wells in the same block for consistency checks.
  • A shared stratigraphic scheme with consistent names and layer order.
  • Well locations and structural maps to evaluate geological plausibility.
  • Historical interpretation reports for cross-checking.

The source material suggests FORCE 2020 lithology data and the Kansas Geological Survey log collection as reference datasets.

sections.title: Difficulty and further directions
sections.html:
Medium difficulty: the task is well defined, but inconsistent label granularity and thin-layer misses remain challenging. Compare change-point detection, sequence segmentation and 1D convolutional models, combined with geological rules.

Low difficulty assumes available data and a clear task with modest error costs. Medium difficulty requires substantial labeling and cleaning. High difficulty involves scarce labels or strict safety constraints and should start with a limited feasibility study.

workflow.title: Case study: automatic boundary picking for 42 wells

steps.name: Prepare and align data
steps.do: Align the curves from 42 wells to a 0.125 m sampling interval and correct depth shifts. Split training and validation by well to prevent information leakage.
steps.effect: Every well appears in only one dataset.
steps.trap: Thousands of depth samples still represent only a few dozen independent wells.

steps.name: Standardize labels
steps.do: Map interpreters’ layer names to a shared stratigraphic scheme. Use median boundary depths and record confidence when layer counts disagree.
steps.effect: Replace inconsistent interpretations with a shared scheme and explicit confidence.
steps.trap: Inconsistent layer definitions cause the model to average incompatible interpretations.

steps.name: Generate candidate boundaries
steps.do: Use windowed mean differences, variance ratios and slopes with change-point detection, or predict boundary probabilities with a 1D U-Net.
steps.effect: Prioritize recall so reviewers receive the important boundaries.
steps.trap: Optimizing precision alone can eliminate thin layers.

steps.name: Apply geological rules
steps.do: Filter candidates using a 1 m minimum layer thickness, consistency with neighboring wells and compatibility with clear log trends.
steps.effect: Turn mathematical changes into geologically plausible candidates.
steps.trap: Strict rules can also remove genuine thin interbeds.

steps.name: Review and feed back corrections
steps.do: Interpreters add, delete and adjust boundaries. Feed reviewed results into the training dataset for subsequent iterations.
steps.effect: New wells provide evidence for improving future predictions.
steps.trap: Without reviewed feedback, the model can become outdated as field conditions change.

workflow.metrics:
Evaluate by matching boundaries

Match predicted and reference boundaries within ±1 m, then count true positives, false positives and misses. Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 = 2PR / (P + R). Mean absolute boundary-depth error is calculated over matches.

The original case narrative lists P = 0.82, R = 0.91, F1 = 0.86 and a mean error of 0.34 m. These are narrative example values, separate from the synthetic experiment’s live calculations.
